claim: The human gastrointestinal microbiota makes essential contributions to host metabolic, physiological, and immune functions.
source: The human gastrointestinal microbiota makes essential contributions to host metabolic, physiological, and immune functions (Fujimura et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fujimura et al., 2010

claim: Aberrations in gut microbiota structure contribute to pathologies and chronic disease states.
source: aberrations in its structure contribute to pathologies and chronic disease states (Houghteling and Walker, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Houghteling and Walker, 2015

claim: Microbiome assembly begins at birth and undergoes dynamic processes influenced by factors such as birth method, feeding method, and antibiotic treatment.
source: Microbiome assembly begins at birth and undergoes dynamic processes influenced by factors such as birth method, feeding method, and antibiotic treatment (Bokulich et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bokulich et al., 2016

claim: Once established, the gut microbiota community is dominated by a core set of species characteristic to the host species and is resilient to perturbations.
source: Once established, the community is dominated by a core set of species characteristic to the host species and is resilient to perturbations (Dethlefsen and Relman, 2011; Martínez et al., 2013; Schloissnig et al., 2013; David et al., 2014a)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The gut microbiota is characterized by a high degree of variation in composition and relative abundance of community members (β-diversity).
source: the gut microbiota is characterized by a high degree of variation in composition and relative abundance of community members, which is referred to as ß-diversity (Huttenhower, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Huttenhower, 2012

claim: Host genetic variation has an established role in driving β-diversity in both mice and humans.
source: Host genetic variation has an established role in driving β-diversity in both mice (Benson et al., 2010) and humans (Turpin et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in mice and humans

claim: A subset of fecal bacterial taxa has been shown to be partly heritable and/or associated with host single-nucleotide polymorphisms or quantitative trait loci.
source: a subset of fecal bacterial taxa has been shown to be partly heritable and/or associated with host single-nucleotide polymorphisms or quantitative trait loci (Turpin et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Goodrich et al., 2016; Benson, 2016)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Most bacterial taxa do not show any significant heritability, and for those that do, heritability estimates are generally low compared to other heritable traits.
source: However, most taxa do not show any significant heritability, and for those that do, heritability estimates are generally low compared to other heritable traits (Goodrich et al., 2016; Hall et al., 2017; Goodrich et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodrich et al. and Hall et al.

claim: Genetic studies in humans show a low degree of repeatability, with only a small number of microbiome genome-wide associations being reproducible.
source: In addition, genetic studies in humans show a low degree of repeatability, with only a small number of microbiome genome-wide associations being reproducible (Turpin et al., 2016; Hall et al., 2017; Goodrich et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The combined effects of host genotype and dietary variables often do not account for the overall variation in a given taxonomic trait.
source: Even the combined effects of host genotype and dietary variables often do not account for the overall variation in a given taxonomic 'trait' (Benson, 2016; Leamy et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Benson, 2016 and Leamy et al., 2014

claim: Monozygotic twins, although slightly more similar than dizygotic twins, exhibit a substantial degree of individuality in their gut microbiota.
source: The rather low contribution of host genetics to microbiome variation and the lack of heritability across many taxa is reflected in studies on monozygotic twins, which although slightly more similar than dizygotic twins, exhibit a substantial degree of individuality (Goodrich et al., 2016; Goodrich et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodrich et al. studies

claim: In mice, the effect of diet on microbiome structure has been shown to exceed the contribution of host genetics.
source: In mice, the effect of diet on microbiome structure has been shown to exceed the contribution of host genetics (Carmody et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Carmody et al., 2015

claim: The contribution of diet to human microbiome variation was estimated to account for only around 6%.
source: However, the contribution of diet to human microbiome variation was estimated to account for only around 6% (Wang et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016

claim: Standardizing the diet did not reduce β-diversity across study participants.
source: standardizing the diet did not reduce β-diversity across study participants (Wu et al., 2011; David et al., 2014b)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2011 and David et al., 2014b

claim: Non-genetic and genetic factors each account for approximately 10% of the variation in gut microbiota and thus fail to explain the majority of the inter-individual diversity observed in human cohorts.
source: Although additional factors such as lifestyle (e.g. smoking), host physiology (e.g. age), and medication contribute to microbiome variation, non-genetic and genetic factors each account for approximately 10% of the variation in gut microbiota and thus fail to explain the majority of the inter-individual diversity that is observed in human cohorts (Wang et al., 2016; Falony et al., 2016; Rothschild et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The timing and order of species immigration during community assembly can cause variation in the structure and function of communities through priority effects and monopolization.
source: With respect to historical processes, ecological theory holds that the timing and order of species immigration during community assembly can cause variation in the structure and function of communities, or historical contingency, through priority effects and monopolization (Fukami, 2015; De Meester et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Fukami, 2015 and De Meester et al., 2016

claim: Mammals are born germ-free.
source: These effects could be paramount in shaping microbiomes as community assembly is initiated for each newborn since mammals are born germ-free (Perez-Muñoz et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Perez-Muñoz et al., 2017

claim: After birth, the offspring gradually acquires a microbial population, and community assembly occurs in parallel to host immunological, physiological, and metabolic maturation.
source: After birth, the offspring gradually acquires a microbial population, and community assembly occurs in parallel to host immunological, physiological, and metabolic maturation, with reciprocal interactions between microbes and host postnatal development (Arrieta et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Arrieta et al., 2014

claim: An early-life 'window of opportunity' is a critical period for both microbiome assembly and microbiome-driven host development.
source: It is increasingly recognized that an early-life 'window of opportunity' is a critical period for both microbiome assembly and microbiome-driven host development (Hansen et al., 2013; Lafores-Lapointe and Arrieta, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hansen et al., 2013 and Lafores-Lapointe and Arrieta, 2017

claim: Priority effects have been suggested to influence gut microbiota assembly.
source: Priority effects have been suggested to influence gut microbiota assembly (Sprockett et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sprockett et al., 2018

claim: Colonization order influenced both the outcome of community assembly and the ecological success of individual colonizers in mice inoculated with two complex seed communities.
source: Experiments in which mice were inoculated in sequence either with two complex seed communities or a cocktail of four bacterial strains and a seed community revealed that colonization order influenced both the outcome of community assembly and the ecological success of individual colonizers
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the manuscript

claim: Historical contingency and priority effects occurred in Rag1-/- mice, suggesting that the adaptive immune system is not a major contributor to these processes.
source: Historical contingency and priority effects also occurred in Rag1-/- mice, suggesting that the adaptive immune system is not a major contributor to these processes
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing WT and Rag1-/- mice

claim: 99.5% of the bacterial types found in the donor microbiomes were also found in the recipient mice.
source: Analysis of donor and recipient microbiota showed that 99.5% of the bacterial types found in the donor microbiomes were also found in the recipient mice
evidence: Supported by sequencing data analysis

claim: 93.4% of the bacterial types in the recipient mice were also detected in the donors.
source: while 93.4% of the types (adding up to 99.3% of the total sequences) in the recipient mice were also detected in the donors
evidence: Supported by sequencing data analysis

claim: The microbiomes of recipient mice had a significantly higher number of observed bacterial types compared to the donor communities.
source: α-diversity analyses revealed that the microbiomes of recipient mice had a significantly higher number of observed bacterial types compared to the donor communities (Figure 2B), irrespective of the order in which the donor microbiomes were introduced (p=2×10−16)
evidence: Supported by alpha-diversity analysis shown in Figure 2B with statistical significance

claim: Higher diversity was observed in recipient mice when species abundance and evenness (Shannon Index) were considered.
source: Higher diversity was observed when species abundance and evenness (Shannon Index) were considered (p=1.13×10−4) (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by Shannon Index analysis shown in Figure 2C with statistical significance

claim: The niche space in the cecal bacterial community, even in wild mice, is not filled.
source: These results suggest that the niche space in the cecal bacterial community, even in wild mice, is not filled
evidence: Inferred from the observation that recipient mice had higher diversity than donors

claim: Most ecosystems in nature are unsaturated.
source: which agrees with the propositions that most ecosystems in nature are unsaturated (Cornell and Lawton, 1992; Pinto-Sánchez et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Cornell and Lawton, 1992 and Pinto-Sánchez et al., 2014

claim: Donor-specific bacterial types can colonize the gut of a recipient host with a 'largely' undisrupted microbiota after fecal microbiota transplantation.
source: This finding is interesting as it provides a potential explanation for why donor-specific bacterial types can colonize the gut of a recipient host with a 'largely' undisrupted microbiota (i.e. patients with metabolic syndrome) after fecal microbiota transplantation (Li et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2016

claim: Hierarchical clustering of bacterial types detected in donor and recipient mice revealed clustering of the communities dependent on colonization order, indicative of historical contingency.
source: Hierarchical clustering performed with all bacterial types detected in the donor and recipient mice revealed clustering of the communities dependent on colonization order (Figure 2A), indicative of historical contingency
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: A total of 395 bacterial types were detected across the two donor communities, of which 101 were uniquely detected in community A, 83 were exclusively detected in community B, and 211 were common to both.
source: A total of 395 bacterial types were detected across the two donor communities, of which 101 were uniquely detected in community A (donor and parents A), 83 were exclusively detected in community B (donor and parents B), and 211 were common to both
evidence: Supported by sequencing data analysis

claim: Arrival order did not influence the number of successful colonizers unique to donor A.
source: Arrival order did not influence the number of successful colonizers unique to donor A (88 ± 6 in A/B, 86 ± 8 in B/A, and 84 ± 9 in AB/AB, F = 2.75; p=0.0521)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of colonization data

claim: Arrival order influenced colonization success of bacterial types unique to donor B.
source: but influenced colonization success of bacterial types unique to donor B (67 ± 8 in B/A, compared to 48 ± 10 in A/B, and 60 ± 7 in AB/AB, F = 26.5; p=8.66×10−11)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of colonization data

claim: A subset of members of the wild-caught B community are less fit than those of the wild-derived A community.
source: These findings suggest that although a subset of members of the wild-caught B community are less fit than those of the wild-derived A community (perhaps because the latter are pre-adapted to facility conditions), early arrival can partly offset this fitness disadvantage
evidence: Inferred from colonization success data

claim: Early arrival can partly offset fitness disadvantage of bacterial types.
source: These findings suggest that although a subset of members of the wild-caught B community are less fit than those of the wild-derived A community (perhaps because the latter are pre-adapted to facility conditions), early arrival can partly offset this fitness disadvantage
evidence: Inferred from colonization success data

claim: The overall cecal microbiomes at day 78 clustered closer to donor A when compared to donor B.
source: The overall cecal microbiomes at day 78 clustered closer to donor A when compared to donor B (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by NMDS analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: Communities from A/B mice clustered closer to Donor A when compared to AB/AB and B/A mice.
source: This analysis further revealed that communities from A/B mice clustered closer to Donor A when compared to AB/AB and B/A mice
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis

claim: Communities of B/A mice clustered closer to Donor B as compared to AB/AB and A/B mice.
source: while those of B/A mice clustered closer to Donor B as compared to AB/AB and A/B mice (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: The communities of the recipients are more similar to the donor community that arrived first.
source: suggesting that the communities of the recipients are more similar to the donor community that arrived first
evidence: Inferred from clustering patterns

claim: Bacterial profiles were significantly affected by colonization order.
source: Analysis of variance of the bacterial communities of just the recipient mice using Adonis revealed that bacterial profiles (clustered on the basis of Bray-Curtis) were significantly affected by colonization order (all treatments p<0.001, R2 = 0.21; A/B vs B/A p<0.001, R2 = 0.23; A/B vs AB/AB p<0.001, R2 = 0.16; and B/A vs AB/AB p=0.002, R2 = 0.11 (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by Adonis statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Cecal microbiomes of mice housed within the same cage were more similar than mice housed in different cages within the same isolator.
source: Cecal microbiomes of mice housed within the same cage were more similar (less β-diversity) than mice housed in different cages within the same isolator (p=0.092 within A/B; p=0.019 within B/A; and p<1.00×10−7 within AB/AB; Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: Mice housed in different isolators had the largest compositional differences.
source: while mice housed in different isolators (no opportunity for dispersal) had the largest compositional differences (p<1.00×10−7 within A/B and B/A; p=6.1×10−3 for AB/AB; Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: The data was best explained by the factor cage, followed by isolator and colonization order.
source: Adonis analysis performed using 'cage', 'isolator', and 'colonization order' as explanatory variables revealed that the data was best explained by the factor cage (p<0.001, R2 = 0.66), followed by isolator (p<0.001, R2 = 0.46) and colonization order (p<0.001, R2 = 0.21)
evidence: Supported by Adonis statistical analysis

claim: Dispersal limitation can cause cage effects even if individual animals acquire exactly the same species members in a completely standardized environment.
source: These results demonstrate that dispersal limitation can cause cage effects even if individual animals acquire exactly the same species members in a completely standardized environment
evidence: Inferred from the cage effect analysis

claim: A difference among mouse groups can arise not only from familial transmission but also solely from ecological drift.
source: This finding has substantial implications for the design and interpretation of mouse experiments, as it suggests that a difference among mouse groups can arise not only from familial transmission (Ubeda et al., 2012) but also solely from ecological drift
evidence: Inferred from the cage effect analysis, with citation to Ubeda et al., 2012

claim: Colonization order makes a clear measurable contribution to β-diversity in the cecal bacterial population of recipient mice.
source: However, although dispersal limitation does explain the largest proportion of β-diversity in the cecal bacterial population of recipient mice, colonization order makes a clear measurable contribution
evidence: Inferred from the Adonis analysis results

claim: 20 bacterial types were significantly influenced by colonization order.
source: However, 20 bacterial types were significantly influenced by colonization order (Supplementary file 1), indicative of priority effects
evidence: Supported by linear mixed model analysis

claim: No significant differences in phyla, families, or genera abundances were observed across experimental groups.
source: No significant differences in phyla, families, or genera abundances were observed across experimental groups (data not shown)
evidence: Supported by compositional analysis

claim: The taxonomic distribution of bacterial types affected by colonization order mirrored the overall community profile, showing that no particular phylum was specifically more affected by colonization history.
source: The taxonomic distribution of these bacterial types mirrored the overall community profile, showing that no particular phylum was specifically more affected by colonization history
evidence: Supported by taxonomic analysis of affected bacterial types

claim: The fact that colonization order impacts bacterial types but not higher taxonomic levels points to the importance of competitive interactions as a major mechanism driving the observations.
source: The fact that colonization order impacts bacterial types but not higher taxonomic levels points to the importance of competitive interactions as a major mechanism driving the observations
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of taxonomic effects

claim: Priority effects were mostly inhibitory, as in 90% of the cases, bacterial types were more successful when introduced in the first inoculation.
source: This analysis revealed that priority effects were mostly inhibitory (Supplementary file 1), as in 90% of the cases, bacterial types were more successful when introduced in the first inoculation (two examples, Types 4996 and 0857, are shown in Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by analysis of bacterial type abundances across treatments

claim: Instances of facilitative effects were observed as two bacterial types (Firmicutes) had a higher abundance when introduced second.
source: However, instances of facilitative effects were also observed as two bacterial types (Firmicutes) had a higher abundance when introduced second (Type_4501 is shown as an example in Figure 4A; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Supported by analysis of bacterial type abundances across treatments

claim: Colonization success of bacterial types was not a function of phylogenetic distance to members of the opposite donor community.
source: However, colonization success of bacterial types (evaluated as the fraction of mice colonized or the average abundance of the bacterial type) was not a function of phylogenetic distance to members of the opposite donor community (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Bacterial functions among gut microbiota members are not necessarily related to phylogeny.
source: This finding suggests that bacterial functions among gut microbiota members are not necessarily related to phylogeny
evidence: Inferred from the lack of phylogenetic signal in colonization success

claim: There were four instances in which closely related bacterial types introduced early prevented the establishment of related bacterial types that arrived later.
source: Although an overall phylogenetic signal could not be detected, there were four instances in which closely related bacterial types introduced early prevented the establishment of related bacterial types that arrived later (1 to 7 mismatches in 16S rRNA gene tag, >97% – >99% similarity; Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by analysis of closely related bacterial types shown in Figure 4B

claim: Cell numbers of L. reuteri Lpuph1 were significantly higher at all time points when introduced on day 5 compared to days 14 and 36.
source: Cell numbers of L. reuteri Lpuph1 were significantly higher (p=8.99×10−8 time*group interaction) at all time points when introduced on day 5 compared to days 14 and 36 (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B with statistical significance

claim: L. reuteri Lpuph1 was only detected at the end of the experiment when it was introduced on day 5 but not at later time points.
source: and the strain was only detected at the end of the experiment when it was introduced on day 5 but not at later time points (detectable in two mice, 1.71 × 106 cells/g of cecal content)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data at day 78

claim: For C. cocleatum ATCC 29902T, the timing of immigration was absolutely crucial, as the organism was only detected in mice when the strain was introduced at day 5.
source: For C. cocleatum ATCC 29902T, the timing of immigration was absolutely crucial, as the organism was only detected in mice when the strain was introduced at day 5 (p<2.20×10−16 time*group interaction) (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B with statistical significance

claim: For B. vulgatus RJ2H1 and L. johnsonii DPPM, time of inoculation did not affect colonization success, and both strains were able to stably colonize mice at equivalent levels independently of arrival time.
source: For B. vulgatus RJ2H1 and L. johnsonii DPPM, time of inoculation did not affect colonization success, and both strains were able to stably colonize mice at equivalent levels independently of arrival time (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Specific microbiota members can differ substantially in the degree to which arrival timing relative to competitors influences their colonization success.
source: These findings indicate that specific microbiota members can differ substantially in the degree to which arrival timing relative to competitors influences their colonization success
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of arrival timing on different strains

claim: The two strains in the cocktail that were favored by early arrival, L. reuteri Lpuph1 and C. cocleatum ATCC 29902T, were 100% identical in their 16S rRNA gene sequence to bacteria present in the donor community.
source: The analysis showed that the two strains in the cocktail that were favored by early arrival, L. reuteri Lpuph1 and C. cocleatum ATCC 29902T, were 100% identical in their 16S rRNA gene sequence to bacteria present in the donor community, Type_3050 (2.15 ± 2.60% abundance) and Type_3983 (0.42 ± 0.15% abundance) (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA sequence comparison shown in Figure 5C

claim: The two stable colonizers not impacted by arrival order had no closely related organism in the donor community.
source: In contrast, the two stable colonizers not impacted to arrival order had no closely related organism in the donor community (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA sequence comparison shown in Figure 5C

claim: Early arrival of a bacterium is critical for its ecological success if the community contains members that overlap with its niche.
source: Although other mechanisms cannot be excluded, our findings therefore suggest that early arrival of a bacterium is critical for its ecological success if the community contains members that overlap with its niche
evidence: Inferred from the relationship between niche overlap and arrival timing effects

claim: If competitors are absent, then stable colonization is independent of timing and can occur later in life.
source: If such competitors are absent, then stable colonization is independent of timing and can occur later in life, equivalent to findings in adult humans in a recent study with Bifidobacterium longum ssp. longum (Maldonado-Gómez et al., 2016)
evidence: Inferred from the colonization patterns and supported by citation to Maldonado-Gómez et al., 2016

claim: No differences in α-diversity were detected across treatments in the experiment testing arrival timing of the four-strain cocktail.
source: No differences in α-diversity were detected across treatments (number of observed bacterial types p=0.464, and Shannon Index p=0.841; Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by alpha-diversity analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: Structure of the fecal bacterial communities showed significant differences based on when the cocktail of specific colonizers was introduced.
source: However, structure of the fecal bacterial communities did show significant differences based on when the cocktail of specific colonizers was introduced (Adonis; Bray Curtis p=0.041, R2 = 0.08; Jaccard Index p=0.013, R2 = 0.08)
evidence: Supported by Adonis statistical analysis

claim: The fecal microbiota in mice inoculated with the four-strain mix at day 5 differed in their overall composition at day 78 compared to those that received the cocktail of strains at day 14.
source: The fecal microbiota in mice inoculated with the four-strain mix at day 5 differed in their overall composition at day 78 compared to those that received the cocktail of strains at day 14 (Adonis; Bray Curtis p=0.047, R2 = 0.07; Jaccard Index p=0.027, R2 = 0.06)
evidence: Supported by Adonis statistical analysis

claim: There was no difference between mice colonized with the cocktail at day 14 and day 36.
source: There was no difference between mice colonized with the cocktail at day 14 and day 36 (Adonis; Bray Curtis p=0.114, R2 = 0.06; Jaccard Index p=0.073, R2 = 0.06) (Figure 5E)
evidence: Supported by Adonis statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5E

claim: Twenty-six bacterial types significantly differed in abundance across treatments in the four-strain cocktail experiment.
source: Twenty-six bacterial types significantly differed in abundance across treatments (random forest analysis; mean importance >2; Supplementary file 2), none of which represented the strains from the cocktail
evidence: Supported by random forest analysis

claim: Differences in arrival timing of just a small number of early colonizers can bring about marked changes in the trajectory of gut microbiota assembly.
source: Overall, these findings demonstrate that differences in arrival timing of just a small number of early colonizers can bring about marked changes in the trajectory of gut microbiota assembly
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results with the four-strain cocktail

claim: The introduction of two whole cecal bacterial communities into Rag1-/- mice led to a significant increase in species richness when compared to the individual donor communities, regardless of colonization order.
source: Equivalent to the findings in WT mice, the introduction of two whole cecal bacterial communities into Rag1-/- mice led to a significant increase in species richness (p=6.63×10−14) when compared to the individual donor communities, regardless of colonization order (Figure 6A)
evidence: Supported by alpha-diversity analysis shown in Figure 6A with statistical significance

claim: Rag1-/- mice in two treatments (B/A and AB/AB) had a slight but significantly lower number of observed bacterial types compared to WT mice.
source: However, when compared to WT mice, Rag1-/- mice in two treatments (B/A and AB/AB) had a slight but significantly lower number of observed bacterial types (p=7.3×10−4 and p=0.028, respectively) (Figure 6B)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 6B

claim: One treatment (B/A) in Rag1-/- mice had a lower Shannon diversity index compared to WT mice.
source: and one treatment (B/A) had a lower Shannon diversity index (p=0.043; data not shown)
evidence: Supported by Shannon diversity analysis

claim: The overall cecal microbiota differed between WT and Rag1-/- mice.
source: In addition, the overall cecal microbiota differed between WT and Rag1-/- mice (Adonis based on Bray-Curtis dissimilarities, p<0.001, R2 = 0.07) (Figure 6C)
evidence: Supported by Adonis analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: 21 bacterial types significantly differed in abundance between WT and Rag1-/- mice.
source: with 21 bacterial types to significantly differ in abundance across genetic backgrounds (Supplementary file 3)
evidence: Supported by compositional analysis

claim: The adaptive immune system increases diversity and affects colonization of specific bacterial strains.
source: These results suggest that the adaptive immune system increases diversity and affects colonization of specific bacterial strains
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of WT and Rag1-/- mice

claim: The impact of early colonization on the similarity of recipient communities to the donor communities was reduced in Rag1-/- mice.
source: Colonization history remained important in Rag1-/- mice, but some differences were detected. The impact of early colonization on the similarity of recipient communities to the donor communities was reduced in Rag1-/- mice (Figure 6D)
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: Only the B/A mice were significantly more similar to donor/parents B when compared to A/B mice in Rag1-/- mice.
source: with only the B/A mice being significantly more similar to donor/parents B when compared to A/B mice (Figure 6E)
evidence: Supported by Bray Curtis dissimilarity analysis shown in Figure 6E

claim: The enhanced level of colonization of donor B-specific bacteria when introduced early observed in WT mice was not detected in Rag1-/- mice.
source: In addition, the enhanced level of colonization of donor B-specific bacteria when introduced early observed in WT mice (Figure 2E), was not detected in Rag1-/- mice, and the average number of donor-B-specific bacterial types successfully colonizing the gut did not differ across treatments (p=0.166, p=0.279, and p=0.980) (data not shown)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of colonization data

claim: The adaptive immune system is a contributor to the successful establishment of specific early arriving bacterial types in the gut.
source: These results illustrate that the adaptive immune system is a contributor to the successful establishment of specific early arriving bacterial types in the gut
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of WT and Rag1-/- mice

claim: There was significant clustering of the cecal microbiota by colonization order in Rag1-/- mice.
source: However, just as in WT mice (Figure 3C), there was significant clustering of the ceca microbiota by colonization order in Rag1-/- mice (Adonis; Bray Curtis and Jaccard dissimilarity, p<0.001, R2 = 0.25; p<0.001, R2 = 0.22, respectively) (Figure 6F)
evidence: Supported by Adonis analysis shown in Figure 6F

claim: β-diversity was impacted to a larger degree by colonization order than by the adaptive immune system.
source: β-diversity was impacted to a larger degree by colonization order than by the adaptive immune system (envfit analysis of correlation between MDS axes and variables; p=0.001; R2 = 0.15, and R2 = 0.07, respectively), indicating a stronger effects of colonization history over host adaptive immunity
evidence: Supported by envfit statistical analysis

claim: Forty-three bacterial types were significantly affected by colonization order in the combined analysis of WT and Rag1-/- mice.
source: Together, forty-three bacterial types were significantly affected by colonization order, with a majority (81%) showing patterns indicative of inhibitory priority effects (Supplementary file 4)
evidence: Supported by linear mixed model analysis

claim: 19 out of the 20 bacterial types previously identified to be significantly affected in WT mice were also affected in the combined analysis.
source: Importantly, those included 19 out of the 20 bacterial types previously identified to be significantly affected in WT mice
evidence: Supported by comparison of affected bacterial types

claim: Only two bacterial types showed a significant interaction between genetic background (WT vs Rag1-/-) and colonization order.
source: while only two bacterial types showed a significant interaction between genetic background (WT vs Rag1-/-) and colonization order (data not shown)
evidence: Supported by linear mixed model analysis

claim: Colonization history remained an important contributor to microbiota assembly from two complex donor communities in the absence of adaptive immunity.
source: Overall, these findings revealed that colonization history remained an important contributor to microbiota assembly from two complex donor communities in the absence of adaptive immunity
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of WT and Rag1-/- mice

claim: The colonization patterns of L. reuteri Lpuph1 and C. cocleatum ATCC 29902T were not different in Rag1-/- and WT mice.
source: The colonization patterns of L. reuteri Lpuph1 and C. cocleatum ATCC 29902T were not different in Rag1-/- and WT mice (p=0.22), and colonization timing remained important (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The population sizes of L. johnsonii DPPM and B. vulgatus RJ2H1 were lower in Rag1-/- mice when colonization occurred later.
source: In contrast, the population sizes of L. johnsonii DPPM and B. vulgatus RJ2H1, which were not affected by colonization timing in WT mice, were lower in Rag1-/- mice when colonization occurred later (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: For both L. johnsonii DPPM and B. vulgatus RJ2H1, later colonization (14 and 36 days) resulted in significantly lower cell numbers in Rag1-/- mice compared to mice colonized at day 5.
source: For both strains, later colonization (14 and 36 days) resulted in significantly lower cell numbers in Rag1-/- mice compared to mice colonized at day 5 (p=1.69×10−5 for L. johnsonii, and p=0.004 for B. vulgatus)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of qPCR data

claim: Later colonization of L. johnsonii DPPM and B. vulgatus RJ2H1 resulted in significantly lower cell numbers in Rag1-/- mice compared to WT mice colonized at days 14 and 36.
source: and to WT mice colonized at days 14 and 36 (p=1.69×10−5 for L. johnsonii, and p=1.33×10−7 for B. vulgatus)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of qPCR data

claim: The impact of the specific colonizers on the historical contingency of the bacterial community was larger in Rag1-/- mice.
source: The impact of the specific colonizers on the historical contingency of the bacterial community was also larger in Rag1-/- mice, as colonization of the strain cocktail at 5 and 14 days resulted in different microbiome configurations when compared to each other and when compared to mice colonized at 36 days (Adonis test across all groups; Bray Curtis dissimilarity p<0.001, R2 = 0.19, Jaccard dissimilarity p<0.001, R2 = 0.17) (Figure 6H)
evidence: Supported by Adonis analysis shown in Figure 6H

claim: 46 bacterial types differed in the assembled community (78 days) of Rag1-/- mice inoculated at days 5, 14 or 36.
source: Random forest analysis revealed that 46 bacterial types differed in the assembled community (78 days) of Rag1-/- mice inoculated at days 5, 14 or 36 (Supplementary file 5)
evidence: Supported by random forest analysis

claim: A greater number of bacterial types were affected by colonization order in Rag1-/- mice when compared to WT mice in the four-strain cocktail experiment.
source: showing that a greater number of types were affected by colonization order when compared to WT mice
evidence: Inferred from comparison of random forest results

claim: The adaptive immune system can contribute to the successful establishment of specific early colonizers.
source: Overall, although the comparisons of WT and Rag1-/- mice indicate that the adaptive immune system can contribute to the successful establishment of specific early colonizers, priority effects and historical contingency still occured in Rag1-/- mice
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of WT and Rag1-/- mice

claim: Priority effects and historical contingency were, in several measurements, increased in Rag1-/- mice when compared to WT mice.
source: and both processes were, in several measurements, increased when compared to WT mice
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of effect sizes and number of affected bacterial types

claim: More bacterial types were affected by colonization order in Rag1-/- mice in the experiments with the bacterial cocktails.
source: More bacterial types were effected by colonization order in Rag1-/-mice in the experiments with the bacterial cocktails
evidence: Supported by comparison of random forest results

claim: Effect sizes in Adonis tests that explained the impact of colonization order on community variation were, on average, higher in Rag1-/- mice in both experiments.
source: and effect sizes in Adonis tests that explained the impact of colonization order on community variation were, on average, higher in both experiments
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Adonis R2 values

claim: The experiments using the cocktail of specific colonizers clearly showed an enhanced role of historical processes in Rag1-/- mice on both the colonization success of the individual microbes as well as the historical contingency of the entire bacterial community.
source: Especially the experiments using the cocktail of specific colonizers clearly showed an enhanced role of historical processes in Rag1-/- mice on both the colonization success of the individual microbes as well as the historical contingency of the entire bacterial community
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the four-strain cocktail experiments

claim: This study established a measurable effect of colonization history on gut microbiota assembly in a model in which host and environmental factors were strictly controlled.
source: In conclusion, this study established a measurable effect of colonization history on gut microbiota assembly in a model in which host and environmental factors were strictly controlled, illuminating a potential cause for the high levels of unexplained individuality in host-associated microbial communities
evidence: Summary of the experimental findings

claim: Colonization history illuminates a potential cause for the high levels of unexplained individuality in host-associated microbial communities.
source: illuminating a potential cause for the high levels of unexplained individuality in host-associated microbial communities
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings

claim: Individuality in gut microbiota composition can arise solely from a variation of the timing by which microbes are acquired.
source: By establishing that historical processes can drive β-diversity of the gut microbiota in a setting where host genetics, diet, and the regional species pool are standardized, this study demonstrated that individuality in gut microbiota composition can arise solely from a variation of the timing by which microbes are acquired
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings

claim: Effects of species arrival history in real life are predicted to be amplified over time and space.
source: Although the relative importance of assembly history appears small in our experiments (and less than that of dispersal limitation), effects of species arrival history in real life are predicted to be amplified over time and space (Fukami, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fukami, 2015

claim: Differences in arrival timing by only four members by a few days can produce a measurable alteration in the long-term trajectory in the development of the community.
source: Our finding that differences in arrival timing by only four members by a few days can produce a measurable alteration in the long-term trajectory in the development of the community is therefore especially relevant
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the four-strain cocktail experiments

claim: Historical events have the potential to add up to contribute substantially to individuality of gut microbiomes.
source: Given that there are hundreds if not thousands of species that assemble into gut microbiomes, most of whose acquisition is likely to some degree stochastic, historical events have the potential to add up to contribute substantially to individuality of gut microbiomes
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings and ecological theory

claim: Clinical and medical interventions early in life (e.g. antibiotics, C-sections, formula feeding) are likely to have longer lasting consequences.
source: Given the importance of historical contingency for gut microbiota assembly, clinical and medical interventions early in life (e.g. antibiotics, C-sections, formula feeding) are likely to have longer lasting consequences
evidence: Inferred from the importance of colonization history demonstrated in the study

claim: Clinical practices could be adjusted to avoid priority effects.
source: driving not only inter-individual differences but potentially also aberrant patterns of colonization that could potentially be prevented by an adjustment of clinical practices to avoid priority effects (Sprockett et al., 2018; Dominguez-Bello et al., 2016)
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citations

claim: Once assembled, the gut microbiota is extremely resilient to therapeutic modulations, dietary changes and moderate doses of antibiotics.
source: Once assembled, the gut microbiota is extremely resilient to therapeutic modulations, dietary changes and moderate doses of antibiotics (Dethlefsen and Relman, 2011; Martínez et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Colonization resistance constitutes a major barrier to introducing beneficial microbes.
source: and colonization resistance constitutes a major barrier to introducing beneficial microbes (Walter et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Walter et al., 2018

claim: Bacterial strains can be stably established in a climax community if closely related species are absent.
source: Our results confirmed recent findings in humans that bacterial strains can be stably established in a climax community if closely related species are absent (Maldonado-Gómez et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Maldonado-Gómez et al., 2016

claim: If competitors are present, stable persistence of introduced strains cannot be achieved.
source: However, if competitors are present, stable persistence cannot be achieved
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the four-strain cocktail experiments

claim: More permanent persistence of introduced microbes can be achieved if they are introduced early in life.
source: More permanent persistence can be achieved if microbes are introduced early in life
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the four-strain cocktail experiments

claim: Early introduction of just a few species can divert the entire trajectory of the microbiota.
source: In addition, the findings demonstrated that early introduction of just a few species can divert the entire trajectory of the microbiota
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the four-strain cocktail experiments

claim: Priority effects will favor bacteria that are introduced first, thereby providing an opportunity to potentially prevent aberrant microbiomes.
source: Although there will likely always be strong stochastic elements in microbiome acquisition, priority effects will favor bacteria that are introduced first, thereby providing an opportunity to potentially prevent aberrant microbiomes, and by doing so, dysbiosis-related diseases
evidence: Speculative inference based on the experimental findings

claim: The age of 10 days was chosen for the first inoculation as it was the earliest age at which pups could be gavaged without jeopardizing their health or parental care.
source: The age of 10 days was chosen for the first inoculation as it was the earliest age at which pups could be gavaged without jeopardizing their health or parental care
evidence: Methodological justification

claim: Minimum Entropy Decomposition (MED) analysis allows the differentiation of sequences with only one nucleotide dissimilarity.
source: by MiSeq Illumina sequencing of 16S rRNA tags using Minimum Entropy Decomposition (MED) analysis, which allows the differentiation of sequences with only one nucleotide dissimilarity (Eren et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Eren et al., 2015

claim: 85% of bacterial types from donor A and 82% from donor B could be detected in recipient mice 4 weeks after colonization during standardization.
source: Cecal bacterial diversity became only marginally reduced in recipient mice 4 weeks after colonization during the standardization when compared to the wild donors, and the majority (85% for donor A and 82% of donor B) of the bacterial types could be detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Recipient microbiota clustered tightly with that of the donor during standardization.
source: In addition, an analysis of Bray-Curtis dissimilarities revealed that recipient microbiota clustered tightly with that of the donor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: A large proportion of the microbiota from wild mice can be established in germ-free mice under laboratory conditions with similar taxonomic distributions and proportions.
source: Overall, these analyses showed that a large proportion of the microbiota from wild mice can be established in germ-free mice under laboratory conditions with similar taxonomic distributions and proportions
evidence: Inferred from the standardization experiment results

claim: The experimental model recapitulates 'real life' conditions during early-life microbiota assembly while keeping ecological variables strictly controlled.
source: The experimental model has several unique advantages in that it recapitulates 'real life' conditions during early-life microbiota assembly while keeping ecological variables strictly controlled
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: The first colonization was done in 10-day-old germ-free mice, which resemble newborn mice as they are devoid of microbes and not yet fully developed.
source: The first colonization was done in 10-day-old germ-free mice, which resemble newborn mice as they are devoid of microbes and not yet fully developed, allowing the study of gut microbiota assembly during a time window critical for both microbiota assembly and host postnatal development (Knoop et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Knoop et al., 2017

claim: The regional species pool is standardized in the experimental model by administration of aliquots of the same inoculum to mice via gavage and maintenance of mice in isolators that prevented acquisition of additional members.
source: This was achieved by the administration of aliquots of the same inoculum to mice via gavage (a highly efficient method of transmission) and the maintenance of mice in isolators that prevented acquisition of additional members
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: Colonization order is the only experimental variable in the model.
source: Consequently, colonization order is the only experimental variable in the model
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: Ex-germ-free Rag1-/- mice develop inflammation in the intestinal epithelial lining in response to bacterial colonization.
source: Ex-germ-free Rag1-/- mice develop inflammation in the intestinal epithelial lining in response to bacterial colonization (Peterson et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Peterson et al., 2007

claim: Stronger selection is predicted to increase competition, which in itself increases the importance of priority effects.
source: Stronger selection is predicted to increase competition, which in itself increases the importance of priority effects (Fukami, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fukami, 2015

claim: The seemingly paradoxical characteristics of the gut microbiota, namely resilience and high intra-individual stability despite large inter-individual variability, are consistent with a view in which stochastic historical events drive inter-individual variability.
source: The seemingly paradoxical characteristics of the gut microbiota, namely resilience and high intra-individual stability despite large inter-individual variability, are consistent with a view in which stochastic historical events such as chance colonization, random extinction, ecological drift, and monopolization, in combination with niche pre-emption and modification (Fukami, 2015), drive inter-individual variability
evidence: Theoretical interpretation supported by citation to Fukami, 2015

claim: Eco-evolutionary feedbacks in which colonizers continue to adapt to the niche opportunities that arise during the dynamic assembly process ensure that communities end up to be composed of highly adapted members that stably occupy niches and display resilience and colonization resistance.
source: Eco-evolutionary feedbacks in which colonizers continue to adapt to the niche opportunities that arise during the dynamic assembly process ensure that communities end up to be, despite their unpredictable configurations, composed of highly adapted members that stably occupy niches and display resilience and colonization resistance (Walter, 2015)
evidence: Theoretical interpretation supported by citation to Walter, 2015

claim: Some level of stochasticity during microbiota assembly would be expected to occur even among monozygotic twins.
source: Since some level of stochasticity during microbiota assembly would be expected to occur even among monozygotic twins, this framework provides an explanation for their surprisingly high inter-individual microbiota variation (Goodrich et al., 2016; Goodrich et al., 2014)
evidence: Theoretical interpretation supported by citations

claim: Low dispersal decreases rates of immigration, which is predicted to enhance priority effects as average time spans between early and later colonizers are increased.
source: In addition, low dispersal decreases rates of immigration, which is predicted to enhance priority effects as average time spans between early and later colonizers are increased (Fukami, 2015), consequently increasing β-diversity (Hubbell, 2001; Chase and Myers, 2011; Rosindell et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to ecological theory

claim: People living in industrialized societies have higher microbiota individuality when compared to non-industrialized populations.
source: These concepts may provide one explanation for the higher microbiota individuality in people living in industrialized societies (which likely have lower levels of dispersal due to sanitation) when compared to non-industrialized populations (Martínez et al., 2015)
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citation to Martínez et al., 2015
